[[File:Centered coloring.svg|thumb|A centered coloring of a graph. Each connected subgraph has a color used by exactly one vertex. The number of colors, four, equals the [[tree-depth]] of the graph.]]
In [[graph theory]], a '''centered coloring''' is a type of [[graph coloring]] related to [[treedepth]]. The minimum number of colors in a centered coloring of a graph equals the graph's [[treedepth]]. A parameterized variant, a <math>q</math>-centered coloring, provides a way of covering graphs with a small number of [[Glossary of graph theory#subgraph|subgraphs]] of treedepth at most <math>q</math>, and can be used in algorithms for [[subgraph isomorphism]] and related problems. The number of colors needed for a <math>q</math>-centered coloring is bounded as a function of <math>q</math> in the graphs of [[bounded expansion]].

==Definition==
A centered coloring is a graph coloring, an assignment of colors to the vertices of a given graph, with the following property: every connected subgraph (or equivalently every connected [[induced subgraph]]) has at least one vertex whose color is unique: no other vertex in the same subgraph has the same color.{{sfnp|Nešetřil|Ossona de Mendez|2012|loc=Definition 6.2|p=125}}

A <math>q</math>-centered coloring is a centered coloring with the weaker property that every connected subgraph (or equivalently every connected [[induced subgraph]]) either has at least <math>q</math> colors, or it has at least one vertex whose color is unique.{{sfnp|Nešetřil|Ossona de Mendez|2012|loc=Definition 7.3|p=154}} For <math>q=2</math> this is an ordinary graph coloring: every edge, and therefore every larger connected subgraph, must have at least two colors.<ref>{{harvtxt|Nešetřil|Ossona de Mendez|2012|p=150}}. The equivalence between the numbers denoted here as <math>\chi_p</math> and the minimum number of colors in a <math>(p+1)-centered</math> coloring is {{harvtxt|Nešetřil|Ossona de Mendez|2012|loc=Corollary 7.1|p=154}}.</ref> For <math>q=3</math> a <math>q</math>-centered coloring is the same thing as a [[star coloring]]: every subgraph with only two colors must be a [[Disjoint union of graphs|disjoint union]] of [[star (graph theory)|stars]], centered at the uniquely colored vertices of each component. For <math>q>n</math>, where <math>n</math> is the number of vertices in the graph, it is impossible to have <math>q</math> colors, and a <math>q</math>-centered coloring is the same thing as a centered coloring without the parameter. More strongly, whenever <math>q</math> is at least equal to the treedepth <math>t</math> of a given graph, the number of colors in a <math>q</math>-centered coloring is also at least equal to <math>t</math>.{{sfnp|Nešetřil|Ossona de Mendez|2012|loc=Lemma 7.1|p=154}}

==Equivalence with treedepth==
The minimum number of colors in a centered coloring of a given graph <math>G</math> equals its [[tree-depth]], the minimum height of a rooted forest <math>F</math> on the same vertex set as <math>G</math> such that every edge in <math>G</math> connects an ancestor–descendant pair in <math>F</math>. In one direction, if <math>F</math> is a forest with this property, a centered coloring with a number of colors equal to its height can be obtained by grouping the vertices of <math>F</math> by distance from the roots of their trees and using one color for each group. In the other direction, from a centered coloring of <math>G</math>, one can obtain a forest <math>F</math> with the desired properties, by choosing a tree root with a unique color in each component of <math>G</math>, with the children of each root constructed recursively from the connected subgraphs obtained by removing the root from <math>G</math>.{{sfnp|Nešetřil|Ossona de Mendez|2012|loc=Proposition 6.6|p=127}}

==Algorithmic application==
In a <math>q</math>-centered coloring, every subset of <math>k</math> colors where <math>k<q</math> induces a subgraph on which the coloring is a centered coloring. This induced subgraph therefore has tree-depth at most <math>k</math>.{{sfnp|Nešetřil|Ossona de Mendez|2012|loc=Corollary 7.1|p=154}}
By choosing all subsets of a given number of colors, any graph with a <math>q</math>-centered coloring can be covered by graphs of bounded tree-depth. In particular, if one wishes to search for copies of a graph <math>H</math> with <math>h</math> vertices as subgraphs of a larger graph <math>G</math> (the subgraph isomorphism problem), and <math>G</math> has an <math>(h+1)</math>-centered coloring with <math>k</math> colors, then any copy of <math>H</math> can use at most <math>h</math> of the colors. One can find all copies of <math>H</math> in the subgraphs of <math>G</math> induced by all <math>h</math>-tuples of colors. This idea reduces the subgraph isomorphism problem to <math>O(k^h)</math> subproblems, each of which can be solved quickly because of its low tree-depth. The same idea applies also to checking whether <math>G</math> models any first-order formula in the [[logic of graphs]] that uses only <math>h</math> variables.{{sfnp|Nešetřil|Ossona de Mendez|2012|loc=Section 18.3: The subgraph isomorphism problem and Boolean queries|pp=400–402}}

For this method to be efficient, it is important that the number of colors in a <math>q</math>-centered coloring be small. For graphs of [[bounded expansion]], this number is bounded by a polynomial of <math>q</math> whose (large) exponent depends on the family.{{sfnp|Nešetřil|Ossona de Mendez|2012|loc=Theorem 7.8|p=166}} More generally, for graphs in a [[Shallow minor#Classification of graph families|nowhere-dense family of graphs]], this number is <math>o(|V(G)|).</math> However, for graphs classes that are somewhere dense (that is, not nowhere-dense), no such bound is possible.{{sfnp|Nešetřil|Ossona de Mendez|2012|loc=Theorem 7.9|p=168}} For graphs of bounded degree, the number of colors is <math>O(q)</math>, for [[planar graph]]s it is <math>O(q^3\log q)</math>, and for graphs with a forbidden [[topological minor]] it is polynomial in <math>q</math>.{{sfnp|Dębski|Felsner|Micek|Schröder|2021}}
